utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the Registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Case number IT-95-8-PT, the Prosecutor versus Dragan Kolundzija and Damir Dosen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I will now ask for the appearances, please. For the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Brenda Hollis, Michael Keegan, Kapila Waidyaratne appear on behalf of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. And could we have the appearances for the Defence, please? Could you introduce yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: On behalf of Dragan Kolundzija, Dusan Vucicevic, from Chicago, and Mr. Jeffrey Aaron, from Los Angeles.

utterances.speaker: MR. AARON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I'm Vladimir Petrovic, and with me is Sanja Turlokov. We represent the defence of Mr. Damir Dosen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I will start by very quickly spelling out our agenda for this particular Status Conference. I will start by reminding all of you what a Status Conference is and what it is that I am expecting from the parties. Then I will discuss with both parties the point which you, the Defence, and you, the Prosecution, have reached in terms of pre-trial procedures. I will talk about the indictment, of course, of the communication of evidence in conformity with the order delivered by the Chamber on March the 10th, which related to the protection of victims and witnesses. We will discuss the communication of other evidence in application of Rule 66(ii) of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and then we will discuss the calendar and the dates that have to be set by the pre-trial Judge. I will then go over the schedule of the trial proper, and I will particularly try to establish how it is we can deal with the length of witness testimonies and what can be done in terms with the links that could be established with other trials that are currently being heard by this Tribunal. Lastly, we will look at all other pending issues before this Trial Chamber. I will ask of the parties to tell us a little more about the accused's state of mind and how they feel; I will turn to the accused as well. And I will try to attend to all other matters that might arise during this Status Conference. As for the Status Conference in itself, I would simply like to remind you what you maybe know, i.e., that the pre-trial Judge has a full role to play, but he can only play his role to the full with your cooperation, and I wish for optimum cooperation between us. This is what is stipulated by both the Statute and our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. As you may know, the Rules provide for the fact that the parties can meet in order to discuss all issues pending in order to try to reach agreements on points of fact or points of law, and I wish for the parties to take full opportunity of this, which is provided for by the Statute and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and I wish for us to try and resolve all matters which the parties do not agree upon. I wish to favour all kinds of arguments and discussions between you, the Defence and the Prosecution. I wish you to reach agreements wherever possible, and you know that these agreements can occur outside the courtroom, if that is necessary; it can also happen in my office, for example. The main objective is to give priority to a speedy preparation for the trial so that the case might be heard as early as possible and in the best conditions possible. We want the trial to be just for both parties represented. So we will try to take stock of where we stand in terms of pre-trial motions, and I will then try to look over the various documents which have to be filed in order for the trial to begin. The first question that arises and which is related to the trial pre-trial procedure is precisely the question of pre-trial motions, and more particularly the indictment. I might have to remind you of the fact that an order has been made by the Trial Chamber on the 10th of February, 2000, and according to this particular order, which bears on the indictment, the Prosecution has submitted an amendment, if you will, an amended attachment to the indictment, and this amended attachment is now officially part of this indictment, and that was something the Trial Chamber gave its decision on. Of course, the Defence, with Mr. Vucicevic and Mr. Petrovic, has followed closely and has, I believe, received all the necessary elements in order to follow closely this particular issue, so you should now know what the indictment looks like. I would now like to turn to you, Mr. Vucicevic, and then I will turn to you, Mr. Petrovic, I would now like to ask you if there are any comments that you would wish to make on that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour, concerning your remarks and your willingness to expedite the preparation of the trial as speedy as possible. We have reviewed the amended schedules to the indictment, and we, at this time, do not believe that that fully complies with the terms of your order. However, Your Honour, in order to apply for a set of preliminary motions under Rule 72, which we respectfully believe that we would be permitted to because that, indeed, constitutes an amendment, we would like to study the matter for a few more days and then, you know, submit our application in writing. But, briefly, as long as -- if I may address the point, Your Honour. There is only a new column, and that column is not directing the type of the activity that the accused has been charged with, because that's basically indicating that the accused has been present from the time that the camp was established to the time that the camp was disbanded. However, the witnesses that the Prosecutor has clearly dispute such broad errorment [sic] in the indictment, and that is only one particular detail that I would -- you know, I wouldn't wish to kind of impose the facts upon the Court at this time. But not withstanding, you know, that every indictment has to be looked at with a view to the facts that the Prosecutor has, the Prosecutor has the duty, under your ruling previously, to tie the acts of the defendant to the particular charges. And I believe substantially, in a form -- maybe there was an attempt -- but in substance, it failed. And we'll address that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Vucicevic. Now, Mr. Petrovic, since you represent Mr. Dosen, would you please like to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we had sufficient time and opportunity to consider the material submitted by the Prosecution, along with their motions, and I believe that this was delivered to us on the 9th of March. We have some serious objections to this, some of them are procedural in nature, and we would like to lay them out for you today, if possible. The Defence for Mr. Dosen fully understands your order, and we wanted to be part of the indictment. What we are bothered with is the way in which something can become an integral part of the indictment. Something that has so many details, that contains so many information, that has so many specific charges in relation to my client can only be made part of the indictment only by the decision of the Chamber or by a formal process of amendment of the indictment, so that it would become an integral part of the indictment. This is my understanding of the process, that this attachment has to become formally an amendment to the indictment. And the only way for an indictment to be changed anyway is for it to be amended in a way which is provided for by the Rules. I would also like to point out something that is clear to the Trial Chamber, the situation in the Kvocka trial. It was an identical type of situation. After the preliminary motions, the indictment was amended, and the changes consisted of several attachments which became an integral part of the indictment through the process of amending it. So the process of the amendment, the Defence was in a position, by filing preliminary motions, pursuant to Rule 72, it was able to test its -- it was able to test the validity of the charges, as it was done in the Kvocka case. There is another reason which I find very important. There are some very serious charges that are leveled against both the clients, and we, as the Defence team, have asked from the Trial Chamber that to be clarified between the parties by challenging the form of the indictment and asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrovic, allow me to interrupt you for a few seconds. If I understood you well, as Mr. Vucicevic has said for Mr. Kolundzija, you also wish to file a written answer to what has been presented by the Prosecution. You are not satisfied by the decision given by the Trial Chamber, the decision by which the Trial Chamber considers that the amended attachment is now officially part of the indictment in this case. Have I well understood what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In essence, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because, at any rate, it will be not be up to the Trial Judge, but to the Trial Chamber in full to decide upon that particular issue. What kind of schedule are you looking at? When would you like to file this written submission on the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No other deadline except the one provided for by Rule 72 for preliminary motions, no extension of the deadline. This is the situation which we treat as a situation of the amending of the indictment, and we only ask for the deadline which has been provided for for this situation, that is, the filing of preliminary motions pursuant to Rule 72.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrovic. Have you finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have several other specific points to make which would contribute to the argument. I believe that in this first part, there was non-compliance with the order of 10 March of this year by the Trial Chamber. And I would not like to take up any more time, either of you, Mr. President, or any other party represented here, but I would like to point out just the most glaring points that -- omissions in this motion. Pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute, there is no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I don't think you've understood what it is that I wanted to say to you. If you think that the Prosecution has not complied with our decision, you must state that in writing. I'll ask the same thing for -- I'm going to ask Mr. Vucicevic the same thing. I asked you when you plan to submit your written documents, your written comments, so that the Trial Chamber can rule, because the Trial Chamber is going to rule on your comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within any deadline which you set out. It could be three days, seven days. Any deadline is acceptable for the Defence of Damir Dosen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Vucicevic, is it? Do you need a time period in order to present your comments in writing?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because we are on our way to a field investigation in Bosnia, and I will be staying there until the 4th, 5th, 6th, as long as it takes, you know, to interview all the witnesses that are available for me there. So, therefore, if I may, we consider what you said in your initial -- in your opening remarks, that this is an amendment process to the indictment, whether it would be an amendment of the text or an amendment of the schedule. In Rule 72, as we understand it, and it was commented on last time at the hearing by the Trial Chamber, this would trigger the invocation of Rule 72 in allowing the Defence to present its preliminary motion. However, in Rule 72, the point that I would only need cleared by you, Your Honour, is -- because Rule 72 provides 60 days after the amendment; however, 30 days after the Prosecutor discloses the evidence upon which the amendment is based. And we have -- on the 9th of April, it will be 30 days since that was submitted by the Prosecutor. We have not had any submission of the Prosecutor based on what amendments were made, and when the Prosecutor addresses that issue, we would clearly have the decision because you could then specify whether that should be 30 days. But we can do it even sooner. I think, you know, we could do it within the next two weeks. Because the common desire is to expedite this, I believe that we can submit this within the next two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to confer with the legal officer. [Judge Bennouna confers with legal officer]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the representatives of the Prosecutor, that is, Ms. Hollis, whether she has any comment to make about what was just said by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, in the Prosecution pleadings on this issue of the form of the indictment, the Prosecution has taken the position that the schedule and the amended schedule were not an integral part of the indictment but rather were, if you will, a variant of a bill of particulars relating to the indictment. The Trial Chamber, in its decision, determined that the schedule would be a part of the indictment. The Trial Chamber then ordered that we file an amended schedule dealing specifically with the culpability under Article 7(1), the capacity of the accused, and if we were alleging that each accused was responsible under both 7(1) and 7(3). We did file that amendment addressing those issues. We filed no additional supporting material for this amendment. We did file it with the Trial Chamber; it was our understanding that we were to file it with the Trial Chamber. But we did not submit additional supporting material, so there is no additional supporting material for this particular amendment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Defence, you have heard what the Prosecutor just said, and if I understand you correctly, you say that there is no substantive issue, no formal problem with the indictment, but rather with an amendment. I will give you time, then, until the 11th of April, in order to submit your arguments in writing, because the Chamber will have to rule in a full bench on that issue that you are raising, the issue that you are challenging, the fact that this is simply a formal change but stating that there is really a problem with the indictment itself, that is, with the counts. I will ask Ms. Hollis, that is, for the Prosecution, whether one week will be enough after that in order to respond to the comments made by the Defence, which would take us to the 25th of April. I'd like to know whether that's all right for you. Are you satisfied with that, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As I understand it, the Defence would file on the 11th, and then we would have one week to file our response; is that correct? Would that be five -- could we have a specific date? That would help clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've made an arithmetical error. I said the 11th of April for the Defence. We've got to add another week. I don't have a calendar in front of me. That would take us to the 18th. Would that date be all right for you, Ms. Hollis, the 18th?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. On the basis of that, on the 18th of April, we will have the Defence position and the response from the Prosecution. At that point, the Chamber, meeting in full bench -- as I've already said to you, since this does not fall under the authority of the pre-trial Judge, who can only exercise what he is competent over, and this does not fall within his jurisdiction -- therefore, as I said, the full Chamber will render its decision in the proper time. As regards that issue, that is, the area of preliminary motions, I believe that was the only point that was raised as regards the preliminary motions, for the time being. I am now going to move, if you agree, to the second point, which deals with the issue of disclosure of evidence. The documents -- on the basis of Rule 66(A)(i), the documents that were presented to the confirming Judge for the indictment were disclosed to the Defence. Let me remind you of this point. They were redacted before being disclosed, and I would repeat also that the Chamber ordered, on the 19th of October, 1999, that is, the order for disclosure as such. In another decision, on the 10th of March, the Chamber rejected the motion presented by the Prosecutor that some of the documents be redacted, and ordered, on the 10th of March, ordered the Prosecution to produce the documents in a non-redacted form within three days and to notify the Chamber by the 17th of March, at the latest, unless the Prosecution were to present requests for protective measures. Unfortunately, the Prosecution has not produced what the Chamber asked for on time. In a moment, I will ask you why. You can explain that to us, Ms. Hollis. And the Defence reacted, on the 21st of March, in a motion asking that that behaviour of the Prosecutor be sanctioned -- that is, for failure to comply with the decision of the Trial Chamber -- and also asked authorisation from the Trial Chamber to interview witnesses. We had to wait well beyond the time period set, that is, until the 24th of March, for the Prosecutor to notify -- to make the notification that it was requested to do. Let me remind you: It is not the problem of the Registry. The Registry and the Registrar have produced the documents on time, but, according to the explanations that were given to us by the Prosecutor, that there was an internal problem within the OTP. This does not concern disclosure of the documents or submission of documents by the Registry. Therefore, this is a problem of communication of documents within the Office of the Prosecutor itself. I consider this incident to be closed now, although I must remind the Prosecution of its obligation to execute the decisions of the Trial Chamber within the time period set by that Trial Chamber, and therefore it is your responsibility to set up the proper mechanism within your office so that documents are submitted and so that execution is carried out within the proper deadlines. The Prosecution has also requested the notification which was sent to us, and in its request, it's asking for protective measures, asking the Trial Chamber to grant protective measures, which are measures with which we are familiar. The Prosecutor was asking that certain identifying data not be disclosed which would allow the witnesses to be located, that is, three weeks to one month before the opening of the trial. This deals with two witnesses, Witnesses N and J. Let me remind you that in the documents which were presented for confirmation, there were only four, including those two, those two witnesses that were presented, the statements that were made during the confirming proceedings. I would now like to turn to the Defence and ask you -- that is, the Defence of Mr. Kolundzija and Mr. Dosen -- to react to the request of the Prosecutor -- that is, from the Prosecutor herself -- in respect of those protective measures for the two witnesses, that is, Witnesses N and J. Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I directly answer your question, I believe you know that I have to kind of continue where Madam Hollis has left off, because on June -- on July 19th, there was disclosure of the evidentiary material upon which the confirmations were based. In your order that you just discussed about, indicated the disclosure of all the material is going to relate to the original indictment and all subsequent amendments. When I reviewed my file, and in reviewing the submission, the most recent submission by the Prosecutor, indicating upon the ministerial mistake that was a full compliance, I realised there was a section 3, "Extracts of Evidence," with the stamp, actually handwritten filings of the Registry, dated June 26, 1995, and the document contains about 105 or 106 pages, even though the last page is number 124, but there are a few pages that were not given to us. There is only -- there is about 42 pages of documents here that are numbered in range 4 to 8. When I reviewed material that was disclosed to us indicating there was only two -- four witnesses, most of these pages are not here. Obviously, when there were other statements of what the witnesses when this original indictment has been confirmed, and these statements were not turned over to us. We cannot proceed expeditiously in preparing this case with this type of a piecemeal approach, Your Honour, and with a view of having this information, our motion for sanction has been filed with your Chambers. However, Your Honour, I have to give you a little bit of a chronological overview. My client, Mr. Kolundzija, has been arrested on June 7th, 1999. Your order was issued -- first order of protection was ordered on October 19th, without any objection of us. Your reinforcement of that order, basically a stern warning of compliance, has been issued on March 10. The Prosecutor yet does not fully comprehend what material was used and what material wasn't used. Prosecutor is asking after the -- one of the witnesses under the assumed name --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the working order, just a moment, please. I think that you agree with me, you agree with me when you say that we've got to move in order. If I'm understanding you correctly, you said that at the beginning that you were missing documents, that the Prosecutor had not given you all the documents that she was supposed to. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: It appears that way, Your Honour, and I would like to tender these copies of the documents that were disclosed to me by the Prosecutor on July 19th for you to view and to find out whether these documents were yet disclosed or not. Because we just received the statement from the Prosecutor that all the supporting documents have been disclosed, so that is a question in issue. I'm putting that at issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what is it that you're missing?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: There was about 120 pages filed with the Office of the Registry on June 26, 1995 and termed "Extracts of Evidence." In those 50 to 60 witness statements, which all of them redacted, only of them were termed "Witness 1" and "Witness 2." The others, they don't have any markings. What I would like to know: Who are these witnesses? Because their release of their names is [indiscernible] by your order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Are we speaking about the same documents? Are these the documents that were submitted in support of the confirmation of the indictment? Are those the documents you're talking about right now, those two? And you should have them in your possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe so. However, the only -- because confirmation of indictment is an ex parte proceedings to which we are not privy. One attempt to amend it before the Trial Chamber has been abandoned so quickly as soon as we filed a motion in opposition of it. I do not know what was here before the Confirming Judge. All what I see what was disclosed to me by the Prosecutor on July 19th, and the section number 3 of material disclosed, and that was disclosed pursuant to Rule 72. There is this material not only that's been disclosed to me on July 19, 1999, I mean -- and this material has been filed with the Office of the Registry in June 26th, 1995. So there is, indeed, a high probability that this material has been used in confirmation of the original indictment, because this case has been confirmed in 1995. Those are issues that I'm putting before Your Honour, and hopefully the Prosecutor can answer, because I believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you very much, Mr. Vucicevic. Ms. Hollis, could you throw some light on that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Let me attempt to do so. When the indictment was originally submitted for confirmation, no witness statements were provided. An extract of evidence was provided; an expert statement was provided. The extract of evidence was exactly as it speaks: It was an extract of evidence; it was not witness statements. During the confirmation proceeding on that original indictment, pursuant to a request of the Confirming Judge, two witness statements were provided. Those witness statements are listed in the exhibit that you have been given as witness statements, two: Witness statement 1 and Witness statement 2. Those were the only statements provided to the Confirming Judge for the original indictment. The material that is listed here in this receipt is exactly what the Confirming Judge received. He received nothing more. And I would note that it was the 16th of July that the counsel was given these materials, and it was the 16th of July that counsel signed for these materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From that point, we now have clarifications for the documents. The documents which were submitted for confirmation were given to you in their totality entirety. Ms. Hollis has just told us that there were two witness statements, if I've understood correctly, only two, which were provided at the same time as the documents that were provided to the confirming Judge. Therefore, you should be clear now about the documents. What I'm asking now is for you to tell us that you have the documents that were given to you in support of the indictment. What is your position on the Prosecutor's motion asking for protective measures for two witnesses? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that Prosecutor is making differentiation between witness statements in its entirety and parts of various witness statements which he is naming "Extracts of Evidence." The Prosecutor is at liberty to submit either the statements in full or in a partial form, but whatever has been presented with confirmation, whether it's in full form or in partial form, as it is called "extracted evidence," I believe has to be released to us in its entirety and with the full names. Because if the Trial Judge, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me interrupt you for a moment. No, no, no, no. I'm interrupting you. The question has been settled. What had to be done in application of the Statute and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence was done at that stage of the proceedings. There were extracts -- well, the documents that were presented for confirmation were given to you as provided for at that stage in the Rules. Now, you must answer my question that I asked you, the question which had to do with the protective measures requested for two statements, two witness statements of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much. And we will review the record of this session and we'll try to find out exactly and have a conference, as you indicated earlier, with you at some later date to address this point. Because it seems, you know, that certain points perhaps, you know, were missed by me, or, you know, perhaps the Prosecutor is using semantics to hide something from us. But, Your Honour, your question directly, you know, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. In order to clarify whether or not you're -- that is, if you are not convinced, you can contact the Prosecutor directly in order to clarify some things having to do with that point, if you haven't quite understood what was said. And as you said, if you have any other clarifications that you want, during another hearing, we can do it then. For the time being, things are clear. The documents which were presented in support of the confirmation weren't disclosed to you, and that's the only thing to clarify in respect of the Rules. Where do we stand now in respect of the question that I asked you having to do with the protective measures that were requested?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: We oppose the request for protective measures as submitted in the present form. The request for protective measures, you know, this is much broader, this is much wider, and this is basically, you know, not contributing any more to the protection of the witness. But perhaps, you know, the main gist of this is to prevent the Defence to prepare adequately for this indictment, which is rather poorly supported by the witness statements of the Prosecutor. However, in a very particular here, on Witness N, Prosecutor is mentioning one of the reasons that he is --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I apologise for interrupting, Your Honour, but if we are going to go into specifics about the motion for protective measures, it may be better that we go into private session so that nothing that is said would inadvertently disclose the identity of a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no intention of going into details. If Mr. Vucicevic is opposed to this, if he is answering no, I will ask him to provide me with written comments, that is, comments explaining why he is opposed to the protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The deadline for responding has not yet elapsed. It was two weeks. Therefore, I'm going to ask that you respond within the deadline set, which ordinarily would be the 7th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'll wait for your answer, and then take my decision, because it is a decision which comes under the authority of the pre-trial Judge, that is, once I've received your answer. I'm not going to ask you to make any oral comments now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I address you only as far as the time in which we -- I'm required to present this? Because it was my anticipation that this was going to be done in an oral presentation today. Since Your Honour wishes the written submission be submitted, and we have plans, we are departing tomorrow for Prijedor and staying there until the 4th or the 5th of April, and upon returning to the United States, I'm afraid that I will not have time to respond, and I will ask you kindly to grant now an extension of time, an additional seven days, within which we could respond in writing to this motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're asking for how much time, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: For additional -- until about the 14th of April, because we will be in Bosnia through the 5th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. All right. You have until the 14th of April to respond to the Prosecutor's motion requesting protective measures. Let me now turn to Mr. Dosen's counsel in respect of the same question. Mr. Petrovic, would you please give us your point of view on those protective measures? Are they acceptable, or do you too, if they aren't acceptable to you, do you plan to present your arguments in writing on that subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will be very brief, but I would like to say something about the matters discussed in the past ten minutes. We have received all the supporting material with the indictment, and that was on the 8th of November. Our only comment would be that we should all consider the rate at which the remaining material will be disclosed, which will be used by both sides during these proceedings. As regards the request of the 24th of March, the Defence is opposed to it and will provide written arguments at a time set by Your Honour. As regards the sanctions suggested, we are not submitting such a proposal to the Trial Judge. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In order to simplify things, both for Mr. Kolundzija's defence and Mr. Dosen's defence, you've got until the 14th of April to respond to the Prosecutor's motion asking for protective measures for the two witnesses mentioned in the motion. And at that point, a decision will be taken on the motion. A final point. Before we move to that final point, it is, of course, understood that if I judge it necessary, I'll ask the Prosecution for a copy of the statements in order to verify that they do, in fact, respond to the objective of the redacted statements and that the reason would only be in order not to be able to identify the whereabouts and names of the witnesses. And lastly, we might as well do it now, since there is an objection. I've heard the Defence objections. I've asked the Prosecutor also to provide us with a copy of the redacted statements so that I could take my decision in full knowledge of what I'm doing. A final point. In the motion that was sent to us, presented by the Defence of Mr. Kolundzija, it was asked that permission be given for interviewing the witnesses. We were requested that by you, Mr. Vucicevic, and from our point of view, I think that I remind you of the relevant paragraph in the order which was rendered by the Trial Chamber, the order of 19 October 1999, which says the following: "The Defence cannot contact a witness or any potential witness whose identity was disclosed to it by the Prosecution, or with any individual whose prior written statements or whose confidential testimony was disclosed by the Prosecution, unless written notification has been given to the Prosecution within reasonable time periods." That's where we stand now in respect of that question. If you want to contact these people, Mr. Vucicevic, that is, in contact with any witnesses, you will have to inform the Prosecution in writing of that. That's what was mentioned in the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: If I may address that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it, of course, is understood that as regards the statements which have been redacted, that there would be a time period set before the trial in order to allow you to get into contact with the witnesses in question. Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are all limited by our time on this world, and since the time is -- everything is measured in time, the time even affects judicial orders; regrettably, but it does. Your order, just as you read, was dated October 19th, and it's five months later, Your Honour, and there is a release of the witness that was given to us, his statement was given to us, that is absolutely favourable to Mr. Kolundzija, and we could have asked for permission to interview him had his name been disclosed to us in a timely fashion, as you ordered. And we would have notified the Prosecutor, but that was all done on the 24th of March, and I departed -- and that was Friday, I believe, or Thursday. And, Your Honour, as long as you have issued that order, I ask you respectfully for the permission to interview that witness and if I could ask the Prosecution, could I use the name, because his name was given to us, could I use his name in open court? Any objection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's one of the witnesses whose unredacted statements were disclosed with their names. These are not witnesses who have sought protective measures. So we would have no basis to object to the use of that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's Mr. Varmaz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speak up, Mr. Vucicevic. But I'm asking you not to address the Prosecution directly. You have to go through the pre-trial Judge if you want to address the Prosecution. It is to me that you have to turn, and I am the one leading the debate now. So now I am telling you that you have had Ms. Hollis's answer. What more do you want to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to get a ruling of the Trial Chamber, because this is a Prosecutor witness, yes, and within the language of your order of -- as reinforced on March 10, would I have your permission to interview this witness, because I am leaving for Prijedor tomorrow, and this witness's name is Suad Varmaz. Also, there is a second witness that participated here on identification proceedings, that was an opening proceeding, and his name was (redacted) (redacted). If I could get your permission to interview those two witnesses. Those are only two witnesses from the Prosecutor's list. Since one testified in the open court, and another whose name was just disclosed to us three days ago. Both of those witnesses have exculpatory statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, would you like to react to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position on contacting witnesses directly by the Defence is that no such contacts should be made until the witness has been given the opportunity to indicate whether they wish to allow such contact or not, and if they do wish to allow it, if they wish to allow it in a place away from where they reside. We believe that the Trial Chamber decision ordering that we be given prior written notice of the witnesses whom the Defence wishes to contact was made in part to allow us to attempt to contact these witnesses and determine if they had objections to any contact by the Defence. We would like to avail ourselves of that opportunity in regard to the two witnesses who were just named by the Defence, to determine if we could contact them and find out if they have any objections to contact by the Defence, and if they would allow such contact, if they have any conditions on such contact so that we may file that information with you and with the Defence. So we could not, at this point, indicate we objected to the contact or did not object to it, without an opportunity to contact these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vucicevic, I would now ask you to simply comply with the order given on October 19th and to comply to this order as is provided for by the Rules. This order stipulates what the procedure should be, and you have not respected that particular procedure. You have not done so up to now. So now I am asking you to go by what is said in the order of the 19th of October. You have to notify in written form the Prosecution of your wishes, and you have to do so in a reasonable deadline, so that the Prosecution may have the possibility to react in good time to what you ask for. So please notify the Prosecution in a written form, stipulate in writing that you want to interview the two particular witnesses you mentioned, and do so within a deadline, within a reasonable deadline, which will allow the Prosecution to take the necessary steps. In particular, the Prosecution will be able to contact the witnesses you wish to hear. Now, that is all that has to be said on this particular issue of the possible interviewing of witnesses by Defence counsel. I will now move on to another issue which is on our agenda; namely, the issue of other evidence disclosure of which are provided for by Rule 66(A)(ii) of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence; disclosure of, among other things, all the statements that the Prosecution wishes to call during the trial, statements other than those we mentioned a moment ago, these statements taken under oath, the affidavits that are provided for in Rule 74 ter of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. This issue has been dealt with by the Trial Chamber in the order of the 10th of March, and the Trial Chamber was convinced that it was up to the pre-trial Judge to set the deadlines that apply to the disclosure of the second category of documents. In this very same order, the Trial Chamber stipulated that the Prosecution could ask for some of its statements to be redacted in order to protect the identities of some of the witnesses involved, or at least to redact the data that would allow anyone to find out about the whereabouts of the witnesses, and it is up to the pre-trial Judge to make sure that these statements are redacted up to a certain date. So I will now turn to the Prosecution, to you, Ms. Hollis, and I will ask you if you could tell the Trial Chamber how many statements fall into that particular category, i.e., how many statements do you plan to have redacted, as is provided by the order I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution regrets that it cannot give you a valid or complete number today. The number of statements which we would wish to redact would depend upon the inputs we receive from the witnesses that we intend to call. We are in the process of contacting potential witnesses, and part of that process is to learn if they do wish such protections. But we have not completed that process. So it may very well be that a substantial number have no redactions because the witnesses have no request for them. It could be that most or all of the statements would have redactions because the witnesses request such. But, unfortunately, Your Honour, I'm not in a position today to give you a number. I will tell you, however, that we are in the process of putting together our potential witness list and of contacting those potential witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, could you, however, maybe tell me now, if you can, of course, how long you would need to meet my request? How much time do you need to give me an idea of the number of statements which might be redacted? And as a matter of fact, is that something that you think you might be able to tell me at some point soon?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have a moment to confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution anticipates that in order to give you a comprehensive response, we would have to contact something in the order of 100 potential witnesses. We believe that in order to be able to do that, we would need five to ten working days to be sure we could contact the greatest number possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said five to ten working days?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would two weeks be enough for you?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Hollis. Which, of course -- I'm sorry. I will now turn to the legal officer of the Chamber, Ms. Featherstone, and I will ask her to help me on the particular deadlines that we need to meet. [Judge Bennouna confers with legal officer]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have already settled on this particular deadline of two weeks, so that brings us to the 11th of April once again. On the 11th of April, I expect you to submit to us this list of statements for which you ask that they be redacted. Of course, these redacted statements have, as their only aim, to avoid the identification of witnesses' names or whereabouts. So your deadline is the 11th of April. Does the Defence have anything else to add on this particular issue that I've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we don't, on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to point out that we need to work out some more specific deadlines as per Article 62(A) because it is very important for the Defence to have these statements as soon as possible, the redacted statements, that is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm coming to that Mr. Petrovic, but thank you for what you have just said. Ms. Hollis, maybe you can help us on this. What is the deadline as far as the disclosure mentioned by the Defence is concerned, disclosure of the evidence, statements and so on?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I may have another moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for the opportunity to consult. As I indicated, Your Honour, we have begun to put together our potential witness list with a view toward moving to 66(A)(ii) and to begin to disclose statements of potential witnesses. We certainly had intended, even before this Status Conference was set, to begin that process in the immediate future. We anticipate that we could provide the redacted or unredacted version statements of potential witnesses within one month to the Defence. This would be the witnesses that we now see as witnesses in the case. Of course, to the extent we don't have confirmation of witnesses' availability or willingness, we might add witnesses later. But we believe in one month we could have the bulk of that done. Your Honour, just to be clear as to what our position is, our position is as we have set it forward in the protective measures motion, and that is we would like delayed disclosure of the names of those witnesses who seek protection. We would like delayed disclosure of their names, not their statements. As regards whereabouts, Your Honour, we would also like delayed disclosure of whereabouts if we have to disclose it at all. We feel very strongly that disclosing the current whereabouts of witnesses puts them in jeopardy of intimidation, harassment, threats, harm, either through inadvertent, unauthorised disclosure, or through, unfortunately, at some times, willing and knowing unauthorised disclosure. So we are very concerned about providing the whereabouts, the current whereabouts of these witnesses. If we are required to do so, Your Honour, we would wish to do so as close in time to the beginning of trial as possible, because the longer this information is available, the more likely it is for some inadvertent disclosure, or even a bad-faith disclosure. So as far as whereabouts is concerned, that, we would not like to disclose until sometime very close to trial, if at all. In regards of other identifying information, as I indicated before, that will depend upon what the witnesses tell us, and we will disclose information about the witnesses when the witness tells us they have no need for protective measures. So in terms of providing the bulk of the information, the witness statements, we believe that we can do that in one month. In terms of compliance with identification and whereabouts, that would be subject to the remarks I just made, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, since you are on your feet, to sum it up, you are asking for one month to disclose to the Defence the unredacted statements. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Unredacted statements for those witnesses who do not seek protection; redacted statements for those witnesses who do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, we're not getting an interpretation. There seems to be a problem with the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: I will try to speak English, if we can save time. If I understand you correctly, I will have a list on the 11th of April, including, I think, the declarations, to allow me to -- including the declarations and the redactions you propose. It will be on the 11th. And you propose a delay of one month from the decision of the pre-trial Judge, I think? Because the question I have, you say, "We need a delay of one month." One month starting from what?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we believe that within one month of today, we could provide to the Defence the redacted versions of statements where the witnesses have requested protected measures, or (2) the potential witnesses that we have not been able to contact, so we don't know what their status is. In addition to that, within that same month, we could provide unredacted copies of witness statements of those witnesses who have indicated they have no need for protective measures. That's one month from today, Your Honour. Your Honour, in relation to the 11th of April, we will be able to provide you with the number of witnesses who would request redactions, but I'm not at all confident we would actually be able to provide you with redactions by that date. I believe it will take us one month to complete that exercise. We could provide you, of course, with the unredacted versions of the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So if I understood you well, within a month, we will be on -- it will be the 28th -- no, rather, today is the 28th of March, so it will be the 28th of April. On that particular date, you will disclose to the Defence all the statements, be they redacted statements or unredacted statements. You will also disclose on the 11th of April, you will give to me as a pre-trial Judge, the list of the statements emanating from the various witnesses, and also the list of the statements for which you do not wish to have the data on the witnesses names and whereabouts to be communicated. And later on, you will also provide to me these statements so that I may make sure that the redactions -- it's much more difficult to say all this in French than it is in English -- that these redactions are under my supervision, under my control. I have to comply with my duties; I have to make sure that you have proceeded to the right redactions. You have to be in conformity with the aim set by the Trial Chamber. And when I receive this from you, I will make a decision on the statements that have been redacted. I will decide on a date at which the whole of the non-redacted statement must be disclosed. I think you've asked between three weeks or a month before the beginning of the trial. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So this is where we stand. Mr. Petrovic, I hope we've answered your question. This is what the situation is in terms of disclosure of statements by the Prosecution. Is there anything else you would like to add? Time is running out. Do you have something else you would need to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a question concerning the process of redaction of the statements of the witnesses, because it is our position that the whole process of the redaction, it's based on the history of our compliance with this Trial Chamber's orders on confidentiality. It is a misguided step that is giving extra and unnecessary work to the Judge, and the final effect of it is creating an unlevel playing field, creating unfair -- it's going to lead to unfair delay to Defence to prepare for the trial and to delay a speedy trial. Indeed, it's going to prejudice the defendant. And, Your Honour, I'm making these remarks with the highest regard for your office and, you know, for the proceedings that we are facing. If I may -- you know, I represented Dr. Kovacevic in that before this Tribunal in 1998, and we had been issued a confidential order on the witness so the protection was the name Witness B. And I have even indicated and presented in the Office of the Prosecutor that perhaps even the fax communication to the former Yugoslavia might be so sensitive, it might be that faxes could be intercepted. And with such issues, we have to be very careful. So to that effect, I've dispatched an assistant of mine to take a trip from here to Banja Luka, to take the name of such a witness and give it to the person who was investigated in the field. No leaks, nothing, because with our high respect for your orders of confidentiality. If we have an order of confidentiality, as strict as you can impose, Your Honour. We could then know about this witness. We can timely apply to the Prosecutor so the mistake of the past, where we are denied the chance to talk to a witness now who is in the Prijedor area, will not repeat itself. And this is going to help us, Your Honour. And one thing, an additional in closing. Thirty days to 21 days, to release the redactions, if you indeed decide to adopt the redactions as a matter of protection, it is so short that we will not be able to conduct any investigation at all. Because first, our office is our man in Chicago, and Mr. Aaron is in Los Angeles. Telephone communication with Bosnia is impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vucicevic, what is it you are asking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking for 75 days, Your Honour, because we have followed confidentiality orders to the utmost, and we intend to do it in the future. We only need a fair chance to defend this man, who most of the Muslim inmates that I've talked to have said that he is -- he has committed no wrong. But, Your Honour, as long as I'm, you know, so moved at this point, I do have to disclose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vucicevic, I have understood what you have just told us, but you also know that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal have been set up over a long period of time. There are a lot of decisions that have been taken on these particular issues, and I'm sure you know about them. So in good time, the Trial Chamber will make its decision on this particular issue that you've raised. Now, swiftly on to the next item on the agenda, i.e., the other deadlines that have to be set by the pre-trial Judge. We all share, I think, the same priority, that is to say, that we want to see the pre-trial procedures run through as smoothly as possible because we all want the trial to start as early as possible and to be a fair and just trial for all persons involved. The 24th of January, Ms. Hollis, the Trial Chamber asked you to start working on the pre-trial brief. I would now like to turn to you to ask you if maybe you can help us see more clearly what the deadlines are. How much time do you need to put this document in order, to submit this pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Prosecution is of the mind that it can have the pre-trial brief ready by the 11th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Hollis. Thank you, because it seems that you have already started working on the pre-trial brief. It is very helpful, because it means that we can work swiftly. I understand, then, that the pre-trial brief will be in our hands on the 11th of April. The second question that I wish to put to you, Ms. Hollis, it is a question which is related to another document which we need within the framework of the pre-trial proceedings, i.e., the list of the documents, the documentary evidence, and the list of the witnesses. At some point, you mentioned some 60 witnesses coming to testify, and you said that you would need about eight weeks, approximately, to hear these witnesses. Could you also give us a date, a date on which you would be able to communicate to us these documents which we need to have before the trial can start?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, earlier, when I spoke, I indicated that in order to fulfil some of our other obligations, we would have to contact up to 100 witnesses. The Prosecution would prefer to be limited by a time in which it can present its case, rather than a number of witnesses, because depending upon what measures are adopted, it may be that witness testimony will move much more quickly. We believe that an estimate of the number of witnesses we would require for trial would be approximately 75 witnesses. There could be some that could be taken by way of deposition, there could be some that would be affidavit-type witnesses, but we believe that 75 would be an appropriate number. Within 30 days, as I indicated earlier, we will have the witness statements of potential witnesses. So at that time, we should have a list of our potential witnesses to provide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what about the documentary evidence, various evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have already provided to the Defence, by way of courier, a list of documentary evidence and copies of the documentary evidence. That is the core of the documentary evidence that we will be using to determine our final documentary evidence needs for the case. So, again, we believe that within one month, we should be able to have what is the most final documentary evidence list we can have, realising that some things are uncertain and some things may change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly I would like to say that in addition to the supporting material of the indictment, the Defence of Damir Dosen received no other document, not counting what I received only today before the beginning of the Status Conference. We discussed this briefly, and we would like -- we will try to overcome this situation, but until now, I have received nothing, no documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, can you help us on this as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, on the 22nd of February, the documentary evidence and some other evidence was sent by courier. It's the Prosecution's understanding that there may be some difficulty with courier delivery to the Defence counsel's office, and perhaps that is why he has not received the evidence. There's not an easy way to send the information to Serbia, but we did send it by courier. But, again, we certainly do not doubt him when he says he has not received it. We believe perhaps that's a problem with the courier service to his office. Also, Your Honour, we have indicated to Defence counsel that we are willing to provide him with another copy of the documentary evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may report that we have received the package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, Mr. Vucicevic. Okay. You have received these documents. But it seems that there may be a transmission problem as regards Mr. Petrovic. Ms. Hollis, you tell me that you might be able to give these documents to Mr. Petrovic now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We've indicated to Mr. Petrovic that we would be able to provide him with another copy of the documents before he leaves on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that's the best way to go about this particular issue. And thank you, Ms. Hollis, for your cooperation. So Mr. Petrovic, I think that you simply have to turn to the Prosecution's offices and ask for these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to suggest, Your Honour, that the documents for the Defence of Mr. Dosen be provided to the Defence here, so that we do not depend on the courier service. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. I'm sure that Ms. Hollis has carefully listened to what you have just said. In fact, I think that these issues on circulation of information, which are technical issues, in a way, can be settled between yourself outside the courtroom. Maybe we don't need to have the Trial Chamber look into these technical questions. We are not dealing with any particular legal issue here. So that's all fine and well. This is, I think, settled. Another issue; it seems that we will have a synthesis on facts and on the -- who will be the witnesses who will come to testify. It seems that we will have this in good time, but my question is: Are the two parties in agreement? Do they agree on the fact that the Trial Chamber might also receive the witnesses' statements, as has been done, I believe, in other cases which have been heard by this Tribunal? I'm turning, first of all, to the Defence bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of Mr. Dosen, of course, agrees with this, and we have no comment on it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, I now turn to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the risk of incurring your wrath, the Prosecution did not intend and does not intend to submit all of the witness statements of its witnesses. We have developed a procedure we would like to follow in this case, and that is when the witnesses come to testify, we would like to provide a summary of, if you will, background evidence that does not deal directly with the camp itself, and that would be marked into evidence as an exhibit which the witness would adopt. Then the remainder of the witness's testimony would be provided directly, through question and answer. Of course, to the extent the statement were used by the Defence to impeach the witness and they wish to offer it, that would be one means of introducing it. But in terms of introducing the bulk of the statements as evidence of the Prosecution, that was not our intention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Hollis. That being the case, I remind you that you have to give us syntheses that are as exhaustive as possible so that we are able to know, in all possible details, what it is that the witness is about to tell us, because this is what allows us to give to the testimony its proper weight. We also make sure that there will not be repetition, unnecessary repetition of some facts or some issues. There is something else we must deal with. It is the points of agreement on facts and points of law, try to see if the parties can agree on some points of facts or on some points of law. Ideally, it would be good that the parties could arrange for a meeting between them, as is provided for by the Rules, a meeting during which they would try to see if they can reach an agreement on some points of facts and some points of law. Also the Prosecution must comply with its obligation, which is that it has to stipulate in a particular document which are the points of facts and the points of law which are in agreement and which are those that are not in agreement with the Defence. I will ask the parties to meet for that particular purpose, so that Ms. Hollis, for the Prosecutor, can give to the Trial Chamber this document that I have just referred to. How much time do the parties need? This meeting should, of course, be organised as early as possible, and the main thing is to tell the pre-trial Judge what it is you have agreed upon during this meeting. So could I maybe give you a month? Would that be enough for you to give me this document I referred to earlier, a document which we very much need to complete the pre-trial procedures, because this document, after the meeting between the parties, establishes which are the points of facts and the points of law on which there is or not an agreement between the parties. Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would suggest that the Defence could not give any meaningful assurances on this matter until they've had the benefit of the disclosure that we have yet to make. In addition to the witness statements that we have discussed here today, the Prosecution does intend to file a motion for adjudicated facts, for notice of adjudicated facts. It would be necessary for the Defence to have that motion before them as well. Since we have set one month as a deadline for disclosure of much of this information, the Prosecution would suggest that there could really be no meaningful exchange between the Prosecution and the Defence until sometime after that, when they've had the opportunity to digest the information given. So perhaps in six weeks they may be able to participate meaningfully in such a discussion, but we don't believe that it would be productive to have a meeting much before six weeks from now, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Vucicevic, I now turn to you. You have heard what the Prosecution offers. It is true that it does seem like a reasonable offer. Before any meeting, you should both have the time to receive all the information that you need. So that can be done within a month. Then you need the time to study all this information, and only then can you attend to this meeting. It is only in these circumstances that the meeting can be a productive one. Ms. Hollis puts forward a deadline of six weeks. What do you think about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I would agree. I think that this is a very reasonable proposal by the OTP, and as you indicated, Your Honour, we would need time to study and constructively respond. If I may add, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I take it that a meeting should be held between you and the Prosecution in about six weeks, starting now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: In terms of scheduling, Your Honour, if you are planning to have another Status Conference, because we do reside and have offices on two different continents, if you could combine those two meetings, a hearing and a meeting in a -- closely in proximity, within the same week, we would be glad to attend both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Petrovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the proposal of the Prosecution is very reasonable. On receipt of most of the material and the pre-trial brief by the Prosecution, and possibly a brief -- or a motion or a notice of adjudicated facts, we would be able to discuss these matters two or three weeks after receiving these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So let me remind you what the decision is on this particular issue. In agreement with both the Prosecution and the Defence, the parties will meet within six weeks, in order to meet with their obligation or, rather, the Prosecution's obligation to establish which are the points of law and the points of fact that can be agreed upon. The parties will also discuss the various points on which they can agree or the various points on which they cannot reach an agreement. Then a document will be handed over to the Judges of the Trial Chamber so that they can see what the conclusion of the meeting is. I thought that the number of witnesses would be somewhat below 75, Ms. Hollis, to say the truth, in view of the limited time frame and the limited geographical zone in which the facts are set out in the indictment, but it seems that there might be some affidavit statements, and it seems also that you might resort to the adjudicated facts procedure. Ms. Hollis, could you tell us: Are you in a position to tell us today, and maybe you can think of what is happening within the framework of another case which is currently heard by the Tribunal -- I'm thinking about the Kvocka et al case -- do you think that some of the witnesses that are testifying for this case could be used for your case? Do you have some witnesses testifying in this case which might come and testify in our case? That's one question I wanted to put to you. The other question I have for you is the following: You talked about adjudicated facts. Do you think of using another case that has been heard by the Tribunal, the Tadic case, to name it, as a reference in terms of adjudicated facts? Because some facts that have been discussed in this previous case are also mentioned in our case, because the facts and the events took place in the same area. Are you planning on using these facts within the general framework of the adjudicated facts procedure? These are the two questions that I put to you, and are you in a position to answer these now?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as to your observation about the number of witnesses, of course, in the proceedings before the Tribunal, not only must the Prosecution prove the underlying substantive crime, such as murder, beatings, persecutions, but we must also prove what we call the common elements of the Article in question. That entails, very often, more witnesses than would be required if we had only to prove the underlying substantive offences. The motion for adjudicated facts could deal with what many of those witnesses would testify to. So to the extent that motion is either agreed upon by the accused and their counsel, or the Trial Chamber rules to accept those facts anyway, then that could obviate the need for some witnesses and reduce the number. In terms of whether we would use the facts from the Tadic appeal decision, yes, indeed, Your Honour, that is what we would look at, as well as some facts that were decided in the Celebici and perhaps some other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as for the affidavits issue, what are your plans? I see that it is translated by "affidavits". That's not exactly what I mean. You know what I mean, this statement taken into very particular circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's possible that regarding witnesses who would testify only to these common elements, that that testimony could be introduced by way of deposition, which would expedite the actual in-court proceedings for the trial. So that is one possibility, and that is the type of witness the Prosecution had in mind for deposition witnesses. In addition to that, Your Honour, regarding the affidavit witnesses that would be permitted under Rule 94 ter, either affidavit or formal statement, that is a Rule which has yet to be, perhaps, further clarified in practice, but the Prosecution would think that perhaps for some witnesses who are corroborating others, that we would be able to find a means acceptable to the Trial Chamber to provide that evidence by way of a submission in keeping with Rule 94 ter, whatever that would turn out to be. In regard to the Kvocka case, the Prosecution trial team you see before you, Your Honour, is the trial team in the Kvocka case as well, so I can speak with some knowledge about that case. We do anticipate there will be witnesses in that case that would also be witnesses to events in Keraterm regarding these accused, and we are contemplating submitting a proposal as to a, perhaps, innovative means by which that testimony could be taken. But we have not yet fully formulated our view on that, so we will be submitting something regarding those witnesses. But it is, indeed, possible that they will be called to testify in this case as well, in one form or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that would be by a means of deposition that is provided for in Rule 71. This, of course, makes it possible for witnesses not to have to come back a second time. It is not necessary for them to come back and testify. This, of course, allows us also to protect the rights of the Defence, among which, of course, is the right to cross-examine the witness, needless to say. So I do hope that we will get from you, Ms. Hollis, a document detailing what it is you plan to do on this particular issue, and I do hope we can get this document as quickly as possible. Can you help me on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we can do that. I will tell you that certainly deposition would be one way to deal with the matter. We were thinking of something that is perhaps more innovative by way of concurrent presentation of evidence, but we will make that clearer in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Is there anything that the Defence counsels would like to say on this particular matter? Yes, Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It seems, you know, this, as the Prosecutor named it, the concurrent presentation of the evidence, we are going back to the joinder of the accused, to a degree. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me cut you short, Mr. Vucicevic. I'm not asking you to argue on this particular issue now. Let us wait for the Prosecution's proposals. We are trying to study the various things that are at our disposal, and in due time, orally or in writing, you will have the opportunity to submit your arguments. This is not the time to do so. It is not the time to argue on a particular procedure which none of us is familiar with. We don't know what the Prosecution's offer will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Excellent, Your Honour. I do thank you for your comments. I just wanted to know that I would respectfully ask you to always keep in high regard defendant's right to cross-examine the witnesses against him, no matter in what forum they are presented, whether it would be in the deposition, some joint presentation, or any other means that you deem fit. But we would like that to be preserved. A quick point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever may be the case, Mr. Vucicevic, this, of course, will be done in full conformity with the Statute and with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Everything that we do here is done in full conformity with our Statute and Rules of Procedure and Evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Just one sentence. My concern concerning judicial notice, because I'm fully aware of the fact findings and presentation of evidence in the Tadic case. I viewed all the videotapes from that trial. However, the Defence in that case did not contend the issues of commonality in the background. The theory of the Defence was a mistaken identity. Therefore, even though the Trial Chamber has passed on those facts, but those facts, with a view of fair cross-examination to the defendant would be wholly inapplicable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the question of judicial notice, we will also make a decision when we will have obtained a clear offer from the Prosecution. Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of the accused Damir Dosen is willing to make every effort to expedite this trial, both by deposition and in other ways, of course, provided that testimony is not admitted unless we are able to challenge it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's settled, I believe. There is something else that I would like to put to the Defence at this time. The Trial Chamber would need to know how long, how much time you would need. We also know that we want to move as forward as quickly as possible. How much time you would need, then, in order to be ready to start the trial. When would you be able to start the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will allow me, Your Honour, to respond on behalf of Mr. Damir Dosen's Defence, it is hard to say at this moment how much time we will need, because we are at the very beginning of disclosure of the material which is to be used in these proceedings. So I'm afraid that any estimate would not really be good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that being the case, what I will ask you to do, then, is that when you receive the documents, presumably you are going to meet with the Prosecutor, as was said, within six weeks, so I will ask you that during the next Status Conference, the date of which will be set in a minute, you give us an estimate at least of the time that you need in order to be ready for trial.
